body.text: In short:
Jim Chalmers says the mid-year budget update will include a "substantial" package of cuts.
The treasurer also says the government is working on plans to cut government regulation.
What's next?
The mid-year budget update will be delivered in December.
A "substantial" package of cuts to government spending will be revealed in next month's mid-year budget update, Treasurer Jim Chalmers has confirmed.

The cuts have been foreshadowed for several weeks, but without any sense of their magnitude. In a speech to an ASIC forum this morning, Mr Chalmers said the mid-year update would have cuts as its main focus.
"It will cut enough, but not too much. It will strike some fine balances," he said.
The government has sustained criticism over the elevated level of government spending, which the opposition and some economists have said is worsening inflation and driving interest rates higher.
Mr Chalmers has consistently rejected that characterisation, but today said the cuts were motivated by economic conditions.
"We take seriously and embrace our responsibilities in the fight against inflation," he said.

No details of individual cuts have been confirmed, but Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said earlier this month the public service would be one target of "belt tightening", and there have been calls to consider means testing for subsidies for electric vehicles and home batteries.
Simpler building code among red tape measures
Mr Chalmers also announced he would write to businesses and investors to gather ideas for regulations that could be cut to simplify compliance for businesses.

He last wrote to government regulators on this matter last year, and told the ASIC forum the process had led to 400 ideas for how red tape could be cut, 140 of which had already been enacted and 200 of which were underway.
"These regulatory reforms span everything from telecommunications to energy to tax, and lots in between ... cumulatively, these changes will make a real difference," he said.
The Business Council of Australia has been campaigning for a 25 per cent cut to the cost of complying with government regulation, which it said cost business billions each year.
The federal opposition has taken up the 25 per cent target. While avoiding a specific target of its own, the government has promised streamlining in several areas.
The ABC understands one such area to be featured in the mid-year budget will be the construction code, which has been subject to consultation with the industry.
The government opposed the Liberals' proposal to slash the building code from about 2,000 pages to fewer than 100, but has promised to find other ways to streamline it.
ATO hits pause on super letters
Another focus revealed by Mr Chalmers was on reducing tax compliance costs.
He said he would consult on a "pre-filling" option for sole traders paying tax and scrapping complex assessments of fringe benefits below $300.
He said these two measures could save businesses $52 million per year.
Mr Chalmers also said the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) had paused sending controversial letters to business about their payment of super to employees.

The Coalition had accused the ATO of "targeting" small businesses with the automated compliance letters, which alerted businesses when their payroll data did not match their employees' reported super contributions.

In a statement yesterday, the ATO said the letters were not debt notices, but were designed to "nudge" businesses to look into possible discrepancies ahead of time, adding that super underpayment was a "serious problem".
Mr Chalmers said it was a matter for the ATO, but that the government had reminded the agency that its "engagement with businesses needs to be respectful [and] constructive".

"Now as I understand it, the ATO has now paused those letters as they improve those processes … The ATO's got a difficult and important job to do, we respect that … Part of that means having another look at these letters that have gone out," he said.
Allegra Spender's CGT fix not a good idea, Chalmers says

The treasurer is also seeking to pass two key tax bills through the parliament late this month, one to establish a 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts and the other to give innovative start-up businesses the option to opt out of the new inflation-linked capital gains tax discount.

Both measures have been highly contentious with business and are opposed by the Coalition, but their passage will depend on the votes of the Greens, who support the government's tax agenda in principle but have raised some concerns.
On trusts, the Greens have focused on what they say are loopholes to exempt charitable giving from the new tax, including money to private schools and sporting clubs.

On the capital gains carve-out for start-ups, which business groups say does not go far enough, the Greens yesterday said they were open to considering an alternative model proposed by independent MP Allegra Spender.
Ms Spender's model would impose a flat 40 per cent discount on all "active assets", using an existing tax law definition to cover assets that are used, or may be used, for business purposes.
Ms Spender has cited analysis from the independent Parliamentary Budget Office suggesting these changes would make little difference to the amount of revenue raised.
She also said this would be a fairer and simpler model, avoiding the need to define what an "innovative'" business is.

Mr Chalmers said he had written to Ms Spender with Treasury analysis on her proposal, which suggested it was "unlikely to lead to a more productive economy" and would be complex and raise integrity issues.
"We had a longish discussion about it ... there are important reasons why I don't think the model that she's put forward is the right model," he said.
